questions.q: Which of these properties must a relation $\le$ satisfy to be a partial order on a set $P$?
choices: Reflexive: $a \le a$ for every $a$
Antisymmetric: $a \le b$ and $b \le a$ together force $a = b$
Transitive: $a \le b$ and $b \le c$ force $a \le c$
Total: any two elements $a, b$ satisfy $a \le b$ or $b \le a$
questions.explain: A partial order is reflexive, antisymmetric, and transitive. Totality is the extra axiom that upgrades a partial order to a total (linear) order, so it is not required of a poset — incomparable pairs are exactly what 'partial' allows.

questions.q: In the divisor lattice of $12$ (positive divisors ordered by divisibility), what is the width — the size of the largest antichain?
questions.explain: The divisors are $1,2,3,4,6,12$. Dropping the global bottom $1$ and top $12$ leaves $\{2,3,4,6\}$. The pairwise-incomparable sets are $\{2,3\}$, $\{3,4\}$, and $\{4,6\}$ — each of size $2$. None grows to three elements, since $2 \mid 4$, $2 \mid 6$, and $3 \mid 6$ each create a comparability. So the width is $2$.

questions.q: A Hasse diagram of a finite poset draws an edge from $x$ up to $y$ exactly when:
choices: $x \le y$ (any comparable pair)
$y$ covers $x$: $x < y$ and no $z$ satisfies $x < z < y$
$x$ and $y$ are incomparable
$x \le y$ and $x, y$ lie in the same chain
questions.explain: A Hasse diagram is the transitive reduction of the order: it draws only covering relations, where $x < y$ with nothing strictly between. All other comparabilities are recovered by following upward paths, so the diagram stays uncluttered.

questions.q: In the divisor lattice of $30$ (which is isomorphic to the Boolean lattice $B_3$), what are the meet $6 \wedge 10$ and join $6 \vee 10$?
choices: meet $= 2$, join $= 30$
meet $= 30$, join $= 2$
meet $= 1$, join $= 60$
meet $= 2$, join $= 60$
questions.explain: On the divisor lattice, meet is $\gcd$ and join is $\operatorname{lcm}$. So $6 \wedge 10 = \gcd(6,10) = 2$ and $6 \vee 10 = \operatorname{lcm}(6,10) = 30$. Both stay inside the divisors of $30$, as a lattice requires.

choices: A lattice is distributive iff it has no $N_5$ or $M_3$ sublattice; it is modular iff it has no $N_5$ sublattice
A lattice is modular iff it has no $M_3$ sublattice; distributive iff no $N_5$
A lattice is distributive iff it has no $N_5$; modular iff no $M_3$
Distributive and modular are the same condition: no $M_3$ sublattice
questions.explain: Modular $\iff$ no pentagon $N_5$ sublattice. Distributive $\iff$ no $N_5$ and no diamond $M_3$ sublattice. Since distributive forbids strictly more, every distributive lattice is modular but not conversely: $M_3$ is modular yet not distributive.

questions.q: The diamond $M_3$ (three incomparable middle elements between a bottom $\hat 0$ and top $\hat 1$) fails distributivity. Why is it still modular?
choices: Because it contains no $N_5$ (pentagon) sublattice
Because it has only five elements
Because all three middle elements are incomparable
Because $\hat 0 \wedge \hat 1 = \hat 0$
questions.explain: Modularity is exactly the absence of an $N_5$ sublattice, and $M_3$ contains no pentagon, so it is modular. It fails distributivity because, for distinct middle atoms $a,b,c$, $a \wedge (b \vee c) = a \wedge \hat 1 = a$ but $(a \wedge b) \vee (a \wedge c) = \hat 0 \vee \hat 0 = \hat 0$.

questions.q: Dilworth's theorem states that in any finite poset:
choices: the largest antichain has the same size as the minimum number of chains covering the poset
the longest chain has the same size as the minimum number of chains covering the poset
every antichain is contained in some maximal chain
the number of chains equals the number of antichains
questions.explain: Dilworth: in a finite poset, max antichain size (the width) equals the minimum number of chains needed to cover all elements. One direction is easy (each chain meets an antichain at most once); the equality is the content of the theorem.

questions.q: Mirsky's theorem is the dual of Dilworth. What does it equate?
choices: longest chain size $=$ minimum number of antichains covering the poset
longest antichain size $=$ minimum number of chains
number of minimal elements $=$ number of maximal elements
width $=$ height for every finite poset
questions.explain: Mirsky's theorem swaps chains and antichains: the length of a longest chain equals the minimum number of antichains needed to cover the poset. The easy bound is that a chain hits each antichain at most once; the partition into 'rank levels' achieves equality.

questions.q: Consider the divisor lattice of $12$: divisors $1,2,3,4,6,12$ ordered by divisibility. Its width is $2$. By Dilworth, what is the minimum number of chains needed to cover all six divisors?
questions.explain: Dilworth says the minimum chain cover equals the width, which is $2$. Indeed $1 \mid 2 \mid 4 \mid 12$ is one chain and $3 \mid 6$ is another, covering all six divisors with $2$ chains.

questions.q: In the Boolean lattice $B_4$ (all subsets of a $4$-element set, ordered by inclusion), Sperner's theorem says the largest antichain is the middle layer. How many subsets does it contain?
questions.explain: The largest antichain in $B_n$ has size $\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$. For $n=4$ this is $\binom{4}{2} = 6$: the six $2$-element subsets, no one of which contains another.

questions.q: Sperner's theorem is proved via the LYM inequality. Which inequality is it?
choices: $\sum_{A \in \mathcal{F}} \dfrac{1}{\binom{n}{|A|}} \le 1$ for any antichain $\mathcal{F}$ in $B_n$
$\sum_{A \in \mathcal{F}} \binom{n}{|A|} \le 2^n$
$|\mathcal{F}| \le 2^{n-1}$ for any antichain
$\sum_{A \in \mathcal{F}} |A| \le n \cdot 2^{n-1}$
questions.explain: The LYM (Lubell–Yamamoto–Meshalkin) inequality says $\sum_{A\in\mathcal F} 1/\binom{n}{|A|} \le 1$ for any antichain. Since each term is at least $1/\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$, the antichain has at most $\binom{n}{\lfloor n/2\rfloor}$ members — Sperner's bound.

questions.q: Why is an antichain in the Boolean lattice $B_n$ the same thing as a 'Sperner family' of sets?
choices: Because incomparable subsets are exactly those where neither contains the other
Because all subsets in an antichain have the same size
Because antichains must avoid the empty set
Because the join of any two members is the full set
questions.explain: In $B_n$ the order is inclusion, so two subsets are comparable iff one contains the other. An antichain is a family no member of which contains another — exactly a Sperner family. (They need not all have the same size, though the extremal one does.)

questions.q: The Möbius function of a poset is defined recursively by $\mu(x,x) = 1$ and, for $x < y$:
choices: $\mu(x,y) = -\sum_{x \le z < y} \mu(x,z)$
$\mu(x,y) = \sum_{x \le z < y} \mu(x,z)$
$\mu(x,y) = -\mu(x,x)$
$\mu(x,y) = \prod_{x \le z \le y} \mu(x,z)$
questions.explain: The defining recursion is $\mu(x,x)=1$ and $\mu(x,y) = -\sum_{x \le z < y} \mu(x,z)$ for $x < y$. Equivalently $\sum_{x \le z \le y}\mu(x,z) = 0$ when $x < y$, which is what makes Möbius inversion work.

questions.q: In the number-theoretic Möbius function on the divisor lattice, $\mu(1, n)$ is the classical $\mu(n)$. What is $\mu(1, 30)$, where $30 = 2 \cdot 3 \cdot 5$?
questions.explain: On the divisor lattice $\mu(1,n) = \mu(n)$, the classical Möbius function: $0$ if $n$ is not squarefree, else $(-1)^k$ for $k$ prime factors. Since $30 = 2\cdot 3\cdot 5$ is squarefree with $k=3$ primes, $\mu(30) = (-1)^3 = -1$.

questions.q: On the Boolean lattice $B_n$, Möbius inversion specializes to which familiar principle?
choices: Inclusion–exclusion
The pigeonhole principle
The binomial theorem
Cauchy–Schwarz
questions.explain: On $B_n$ the Möbius function is $\mu(A,B) = (-1)^{|B \setminus A|}$ for $A \subseteq B$, so Möbius inversion $f(x) = \sum_{y \le x}\mu(y,x)g(y)$ becomes the alternating-sign inclusion–exclusion formula. The divisor lattice version recovers classical number-theoretic Möbius inversion.

questions.q: What distinguishes a complete lattice from an ordinary lattice?
choices: Every subset (not just every pair) has a meet and a join
It is finite
It is distributive
It has no infinite chains
questions.explain: A lattice guarantees meets and joins of finite (in particular two-element) subsets. A complete lattice strengthens this to arbitrary subsets, including infinite ones — which in particular gives a global bottom $\hat 0 = \bigwedge L$ and top $\hat 1 = \bigvee L$.

questions.q: The Knaster–Tarski theorem says that a monotone (order-preserving) map $f$ on a complete lattice $L$ has a least fixed point equal to:
choices: $\bigwedge \{ x : f(x) \le x \}$, the meet of all pre-fixed points
$\bigvee \{ x : x \le f(x) \}$, the join of all post-fixed points
the bottom element $\hat 0$ always
the unique $x$ with $f(x) = x$
questions.explain: Knaster–Tarski: the set of fixed points of a monotone $f$ on a complete lattice is itself a complete lattice. The least fixed point is $\bigwedge\{x : f(x) \le x\}$, the meet of all pre-fixed points; dually the greatest is the join of all post-fixed points. Fixed points need not be unique.

questions.q: Select every true statement about Knaster–Tarski and order-theoretic fixed points.
choices: Monotonicity of $f$, not continuity, is what the theorem requires
The fixed points of $f$ form a complete lattice, so a least and a greatest fixed point always exist
It applies to any complete lattice, including infinite ones
Unlike the Banach fixed-point theorem, it needs a metric and a contraction
questions.explain: Knaster–Tarski needs only monotonicity on a complete lattice (no metric, no contraction, no continuity), and it guarantees a whole complete lattice of fixed points — hence a least and greatest. That is precisely the contrast with Banach's theorem, which is metric and yields a unique fixed point; so the fourth statement is false.
